title: Yves Congar
hookLine: a Dominican once silenced, later an architect of Vatican II

lines: LATER: A SEAT AT THE COUNCIL.
cards: A French friar packs a suitcase. He is a scholar of the Church, a man who lives among books and footnotes, and he has just been told by his superiors, under pressure from Rome, that he may no longer teach.
What he writes now must be checked before anyone reads it. He is sent away from Paris, from his students, from his work. He doesn't storm off.
He doesn't leave the order. He goes. Years later, the same man would sit in the hall of a council of the whole Church, helping bishops write the documents they would vote on.

teach.h: WHAT IS THE CHURCH, AND HOW DOES IT RENEW?
teach.b: Yves Congar was a Dominican theologian who spent his life on one large question: what is the Church, and how does it renew itself without losing itself?
He wrote about reform, about the role of laypeople, about Christians of other churches as brothers and sisters to be listened to. One of his books is called True and False Reform in the Church.
In his time some of these ideas looked dangerous to authorities in Rome, and he was restricted: no teaching, no publishing without permission, sent from place to place.
His journals, published after his death, show how much it hurt.
And yet he obeyed. Not because he thought he was wrong, but because, for him, staying inside the Church was part of what reform meant. True reform, he argued, is patient.
It doesn't break the body to heal it. Then the wind changed.

teach.h: CALLED IN AS AN EXPERT AT VATICAN II.
teach.b: Pope John the Twenty-Third called the Second Vatican Council, and Congar was brought in as an expert. Ideas he had been silenced for helped shape what the council wrote about the Church and about other Christians.
Near the end of his life, Pope John Paul II made him a cardinal.
The letter of James, in the Douay-Rheims, has a farmer for this: "Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth: patiently bearing till he receive the early and latter rain."
You plant, and you wait for weather you don't control. Patience is not the same as giving up.

how: Catholic theologians and students still read Congar on the Church, the laity and Christian unity, and his name comes up often when Catholics talk about how Vatican II's teaching took shape.

games.q: you're Congar. Rome has restricted your teaching, and you believe your ideas are right. what do you do?
o: leave the order and publish anyway.
games.why: he obeyed and kept working. later he was called to the council and, near the end of his life, made a cardinal.

practice: Bring to mind one place where you feel misread right now, and let yourself feel the sting for a moment without arguing your case.

Then picture the farmer in James at the edge of a planted field, looking at the sky: the planting is done, and the rain isn't yours to command. If you pray, hand the misunderstanding over to God for now.

wordCard.voice: Yves Congar. The Dominican theologian who was silenced, obeyed, and later helped shape the Second Vatican Council. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: an expert. The title of the theologians who advised the bishops at Vatican II, Congar among them.

carryVoice: Your line: vindicated later. Congar waited for a rain he couldn't command. Rest well.
